prompt.en: A VHF signal stays close to the surface because the lower atmosphere bends it gently. Which label best separates that path from ground wave?

text.en: Tropospheric wave, because lower-atmosphere bending is the key effect.
Ground wave, because any path near Earth must be controlled by surface current.
Ionospheric wave, because all bending paths use the upper atmosphere.
Meteor scatter, because any VHF signal beyond the horizon must use a trail.

explanation.en: Tropospheric wave points to bending in the lower atmosphere. Ground wave follows and is affected by the surface itself, so the two labels are not interchangeable.

prompt.en: A VHF event shifts from brief shower-related pings to a steadier path along a lake inversion. Which operating adjustment best fits the change?

text.en: Schedule long overs for the pings, because short reflections leave more time than inversion paths.
Treat the ping period as short contact windows, then use more normal exchange timing while the inversion path stays steady.
Log both as the same kind of ionospheric opening because the band is VHF.
Ignore timing once the first contact is made; both openings should last the same length.

explanation.en: Meteor-related pings are brief, so timing must be concise. A duct or enhanced lower-atmosphere path can allow more normal exchanges while the weather structure persists, but it still may fade.

prompt.en: An HF station hears weak, smeared signals from inside the expected skip zone while operating near the path's upper usable limit. Which explanation best fits?

text.en: Scatter is becoming noticeable because the main returned path is marginal near the MUF.
Ordinary ground wave is strongest near the MUF and always fills the skip zone.
Line-of-sight propagation has replaced the ionosphere, so height no longer matters.
Ducting in the lower atmosphere is the only possible source of weak HF audio.

explanation.en: Near the MUF, the main sky-wave path may be weak and the skip zone may be wide. Small amounts of scattered energy can then be heard as weak, distorted signals.
